title: Capacity Orchestra and Commit Tiling PRD (draft)
content:
Executive summary:

This draft introduces two orthogonal primitives for Dedicated capacity that together provide more predictable economic and performance outcomes for tenants: 1) Commit Tiling — a temporal/fractional reservation model that slices tenant commitments into staggered "tiles" to enable fractional reservations, phased commit changes, and low-friction seasonal toggles; and 2) Safety Margin Orchestra — a runtime orchestration layer that composes warm pools, soft-fallback lanes, and hedged burst policies to guarantee latency SLOs while minimizing the committed footprint.

Why this idea now:
- Customers increasingly want lower commitment floors (fractional months, seasonal bursts) but don’t want increased noisy-neighbor risk.
- Existing reserved-capacity semantics are all-or-nothing at billing cadence boundaries and force large warm pools or expensive burst credits.
- We can combine subtle economic primitives with runtime routing to unlock higher utilization and better SLO compliance.

Goals:
- Reduce effective committed GPU-hours needed to meet 95th/99th latency SLOs by enabling temporally-shifted tile commitments and coordinated warm-pool orchestration.
- Provide clear tenant controls: commit granularity, fidelity lanes, auto-hedging preferences, and graceful fallbacks.
- Keep operator complexity manageable (observability, simulation-first rollout).

Non-goals:
- Immediate change to billing primitives (billing follow-on to product/finance).
- Replace existing hard-reservation offerings for customers that require physical isolation.

User personas and stories:
- Platform engineer at a mid-size SaaS company: "I want to drop my monthly reserved commit by 30% and still hit daytime peak SLAs using automated warm-pools and tiling so I can reduce cash commitments."
- Growth-stage startup: "We need temporary capacity spikes for campaigns and would rather buy short tiles than overcommit for three months."
- Redwood internal SRE/operator: "I need clear telemetry and failure modes to operate commit-tiling safely across many tenants."

Key concepts (novel primitives):
1) Commit Tiling
- Description: Break a tenant's reserved commitment into a set of time-windowed tiles (e.g., 1-day, 1-week, or 1-month tiles). Tiles can overlap, stagger, or be fractional (e.g., 20% of a GPU cluster for 72 hours).
- Properties: tiles have start/end, fidelity weight (how much capacity they promise), and prewarm policy (immediate, staged, lazy).
- Tenant controls: create/delete tile, set target SLOs per tile, transfer tiles between regions.
- Operator controls: set tenant max-tiling-coverage (policy), throttles, and safety budgets.

2) Safety Margin Orchestra
- Description: A coordinating controller that composes multiple mitigation instruments against the committed footprint: warm pools, hedged burst lanes, soft-fallback lightweight models, and cache-prefetching. The Orchestra runs policy that decides which instrument to use for any request based on latency budget, cost budget, and fidelity lane.
- Properties: policy-driven, pluggable instruments, observable decisions.

3) Fidelity Lanes
- Definition: logical class labels for tenant traffic representing strictness of SLO/cost sensitivity (e.g., platinum/high-fidelity, gold/standard, bronze/best-effort). Each lane maps to routing/hedging behavior.

Design overview:
- Reservation model: tenants buy a baseline reservation (same as today) but can optionally enable tiling on top of it. Tiling is represented in the control plane as a set of active tiles; billing remains tied to the aggregate committed time until finance decides to change pricing.
- Runtime: requests are assigned a fidelity lane. The Safety Margin Orchestra inspects the current capacity state and tile coverage and chooses: serve on committed pool, prewarm a tile (if available), use hedged burst (dedicated spare pool), fall back to hosted-compatible model variant, or queue.
- Isolation controls: we introduce a soft-isolation envelope per tenant which is enforced by orchestration: maximum hedged-burst consumption, prewarm concurrency caps, and eviction priority keys.

APIs and tenant UX (sketch):
- Tile lifecycle API: create_tile(tenant_id, start, end, fraction, prewarm_policy, fidelity_lane) -> tile_id
- Query API: list_tiles(tenant_id) -> [tile metadata]
- Policy flags: enable_commit_tiling, max_fractional_commit, fidelity_defaults
- Console: timeline view with tiles, predicted cost delta, SLO risk chart, and quick toggle to convert an existing monthly commit into tiled coverage.

Operator and SRE controls:
- Tenant safety budget ledger: tracks recent hedged-burst spend per tenant and enforces decay/repayment rules.
- Auto-throttle rules: global and per-tenant headroom thresholds that reduce prewarm aggressiveness when cluster occupancy high.
- Circuit-breakers: hard eviction on severe contention; controlled draining and tenant notification hooks.
- Simulation mode: dry-run policy simulator that evaluates tile placement and orchestra decisions against historical traces.

Telemetry and metrics:
- Per-tenant: tile-coverage %, average prewarm latency, hedged-burst consumption (GPU-minutes), SLO hit rate by fidelity lane, cost delta vs baseline reservation.
- Cluster-level: warm-pool occupancy, tile churn, replayed simulator mismatch %, eviction events.
- Alerts: rising hedged-burst spend rate, repeated fidelity-lane degradations, cross-tenant contamination signals.

Safety and failure modes:
- Risk: overlapping tiles across tenants could accidentally create high contention at boundary times. Mitigation: admission control + lookahead scheduler + operator override.
- Risk: misconfigured prewarm policy causing cold-start latency spikes. Mitigation: default conservative prewarm, canary on small set of tenants, simulator tests.
- Risk: tenants gaming fidelity lanes to reduce cost while requiring high latency. Mitigation: lane quarantine, billing reconciliation, and periodic fidelity audits.

Metrics for success (60–90 day):
- 20–35% reduction in committed GPU-hours for participating tenants without degrading 99th latency by >5% for high-fidelity lanes.
- Simulator-predicted SLO compliance within 10% of observed for 95th/99th windows.
- Operator tooling can surface and resolve tile collisions within 15 minutes median.

Rollout plan (phases):
1) Simulation & backend-only prototype (2–4 weeks): implement tile model + orchestra simulator run on 6 months of historical traffic for a handful of pilot tenants.
2) Internal pilot (4–6 weeks): expose tile creation to internal teams and a small set of trusted customers, conservative defaults, telemetry dashboards.
3) Beta (8–12 weeks): public beta, limited region, UI controls, feature flags for finance/billing.
4) General availability (pending billing integration & ops runbook): full productization and performance SLAs.

Open questions / decisions required:
- Billing: should we bill tiles as pro-rata reservations or treat them as operational credits? Finance input needed.
- Tile minimal granularity: 1 day vs 1 week — tradeoffs: billing complexity vs operational churn.
- Default fidelity mapping and enforcement: who sets the mapping in multi-tenant orgs?

Next steps:
- Product: finalize API spec and console mockups (owner: Avery Chen).
- Applied ML/Serving: prototype simulator hooks and warm-pool prewarm policies (owner: Noah Ruiz).
- SRE: draft operator runbook for eviction and ledger reconciliation (owner: Sofia Martinez).
- Finance: quick sync to decide billing model options (owner: Maya Patel).

Appendix: short example flow
- Tenant creates a baseline 10-GPU monthly reservation. They enable tiling and add three 72-hour tiles at 30% each staggered across the month. The Safety Margin Orchestra routes daytime requests to committed pool, prewarms the next-day tile in the evening, and uses a small hedged-burst pool if a sudden campaign brings traffic above prewarmed capacity. The tenant reduces baseline commit to 7 GPUs and still maintains 99th latency for platinum lane due to the combined tactics.
